claims.text: In situ preheating during additive manufacturing of high-entropy-alloy components reduces thermal gradients.
Reduced thermal gradients lessen residual stresses in additively manufactured HEA components.
In situ preheating promotes a more uniform microstructure in additively manufactured HEA components.
HEA components produced by conventional AM without preheating typically experience rapid-cooling-induced thermal gradients and residual stresses.
HEA components produced by conventional AM without preheating typically exhibit dimensional distortion.
HEA components produced by conventional AM without preheating typically exhibit porosity and microcracks.
Preheating reduces temperature differentials and cooling rates during deposition.
Lower cooling rates diminish residual-stress buildup and refine the microstructure.
Preheating moderates the thermal gradient between successive deposited layers and slows rapid, uneven solidification.
Controlled cooling caused by preheating minimizes residual-stress development.
Controlled cooling caused by preheating reduces the nucleation of pores and microcracks.
Relative to an ambient-temperature baseline, preheating improves dimensional accuracy by reducing warping and shrinkage.
Relative to an ambient-temperature baseline, preheating increases both strength and ductility.
Relative to an ambient-temperature baseline, preheating reduces fabrication-induced defect occurrence.
AM process parameters influence the likelihood of printing defects, so the benefits of preheating may depend on parameter optimization.
Insufficient preheating may fail to mitigate defects.
Excessive preheating may cause grain coarsening or unwanted phase transformations.
The efficacy and magnitude of improvement from preheating vary with HEA composition and processing conditions.
